cards.title: Set Up a Local AI Coding Environment for Shopify Theme Edits
cards.summary: Prepare an AI coding workspace for Shopify theme work, checking current tool access and editing an unpublished theme copy.
cards.use_when: You want to make custom theme or product-page edits (new blocks, modified cart, custom templates) without hiring a developer or adding apps.
steps: Verify current Claude Code access, authentication and billing options before buying a plan. The tutorial used a paid Claude plan; its plan-access claim is point-in-time.
Download and install Visual Studio Code (free).
In VS Code, use File > Open Folder to create and open an empty directory named something like 'Shopify editor'; this folder becomes the environment where theme files and connections live.
Open the Extensions panel, search 'Claude', and install the extension published by Anthropic (ignore other similarly named extensions).
Click the Claude button in the top-right to open the Claude chat panel inside VS Code; the left sidebar shows your files, the chat panel is the main work area.
Verify the current Claude/VS Code extension interface and menu locations at install time, since extension UI and plan names change.
caveats: Install only the Anthropic-published extension among the many search results.
This sets up the tooling; it does not guarantee conversion improvements on its own.
Use an unpublished theme copy and preview changes before making them live.

cards.title: Connect Shopify CLI and Authenticate Your Store
cards.summary: Have Claude install the Shopify CLI (NPM version) and authenticate your store so it can list and pull themes.
cards.use_when: Your local Claude/VS Code environment is set up but not yet connected to your Shopify store, so you need it to see and pull themes.
steps: Prompt Claude to install the Shopify CLI (command line interface) — this is the tool that lets Claude talk to your store.
When asked how to install, choose the NPM version. The presenter reports the Homebrew version failed for them; treat this as a situational preference, not a universal rule.
Approve the installation prompts as they appear, checking each one before allowing.
Prompt Claude to 'connect to my Shopify store and give me a list of the themes' — this triggers authentication.
Provide the store URL when asked, then copy the authentication command Claude gives you (e.g. 'shopify auth login') into a new VS Code terminal and run it.
Choose the correct account in the terminal prompt; a browser authentication screen may appear on some setups.
Once authenticated, confirm Claude can list your themes (the presenter's store showed 13).
Verify current CLI install options and login command in the Shopify CLI docs, since these change.
caveats: Claude cannot authenticate on your behalf for security reasons; you complete login manually in the terminal.
Ask for the theme list first to confirm the connection before editing anything.

cards.title: Duplicate the Live Theme Before Any AI Editing
cards.summary: Create a copy of the live theme and confine all edits to that copy to avoid breaking the storefront.
cards.use_when: You are about to make any AI-driven theme change and need a safe staging environment.
steps: After connecting, prompt Claude to 'duplicate the live theme' — the presenter's result was called 'copy of horizon'.
Immediately instruct Claude to 'continue to work just on that theme' so every subsequent edit targets the copy.
Confirm the duplicated theme appears under Online Store > Themes in Shopify (the copy is created on the store as well as pulled locally).
Verify all theme files are now pulled into your local folder so edits happen against the copy's code.
Treat the live theme as untouchable until the edited copy is validated and published.
caveats: Editing a live theme risks breaking the entire storefront if something goes wrong.
Do not skip the 'work only on that theme' instruction — otherwise Claude may target the wrong theme.

cards.title: Inject an Editable Objection-Busting Trust Block Under Add to Cart
cards.summary: Prompt Claude to add a reusable theme-editor block of trust icons and text directly below the buy buttons.
cards.use_when: Your product page lacks shipping, guarantee and returns reassurance near the add-to-cart button and you want it editable without an app.
steps: Identify the template to edit (e.g. the default product template) in the theme editor.

Prompt Claude with specifics, e.g.: 'In the product page default template, underneath the add-to-cart button, add three icons and text I can edit in the theme editor — one for shipping, one for guarantees, one for returns.'
Optionally approve all edits for the session to avoid confirming each change individually.
Wait for Claude to report what it built (the example produced delivery truck, shield and refresh-arrow icons).
In the theme editor, refresh the template and confirm a new block (named something like 'Product Trust Buttons') appears, is movable/reorderable, and its icons and text are editable.
Replicate the pattern for other repeated reassurance needs (payment icons, sizing notes).
caveats: This is more capable than Shopify's Sidekick, which the presenter says can essentially only generate sections — Claude Code can add editable blocks and templates.
Build time in the example was roughly one to two minutes; longer prompts or many instructions can fail (see the one-change-at-a-time caveat).

cards.title: Generate a Full High-Converting Product Template from a Framework Document
cards.summary: Upload a product-page framework to Claude and have it code an entire reusable template with standard conversion sections.
cards.use_when: You want a structured, reusable PDP template beyond what your default theme ships with, and you already have a page anatomy/framework to follow.
steps: Have your product-page framework document ready (the presenter uses a 'Perfect Product Page' framework covering hero, trust badges, benefits grid, outcome, image+text, feature highlight and social proof).
Prompt Claude: 'Create a brand new product template in this theme using the attached framework,' and upload the document.
Let Claude analyze the framework and generate the template; the example took a couple of minutes.
In Shopify, refresh and confirm a new template (labeled e.g. 'PPP') exists on the duplicate theme.
Treat the generated template as a baseline outline to refine: toggle sections on/off, resize icons, remove duplicated elements (the presenter hid a redundant benefits grid).
Use the theme editor's section settings (badge position, swatch style, etc.) to configure the template per product.
Assign the template to products where it fits, or duplicate it for testing.
caveats: The generated layout is a starting outline, not a finished page — expect to edit and remove redundant sections.
Don't assume the framework itself will translate into conversion gains without testing.

cards.title: Clone a Competitor Design Element via Screenshot
cards.summary: Paste a screenshot of a competitor feature into Claude and have it build a matching, customizable component on your store.
cards.use_when: You spot a specific high-performing UI element (e.g. a 'Top Seller' badge on a swatch) on a competitor's store and want an equivalent on your PDP.
steps: Find the element on the competitor's site (the example is True Classic's 'Top Seller' heart badge on a variant swatch).
Screenshot or copy that section.

Attach the image to Claude with a prompt like: 'Using the attached reference image, add a similar badge... to my swatches on my product page. I need to add an icon, change the text and color, but the styling must look exactly the same as the reference image.'
Let Claude build the component; it will return setup instructions (the example added a 'Swatch label' block with an emoji/icon and color options).
Apply it in the theme editor: click Add block > Swatch label, and set the option/option value to match the variant name exactly.
Customize the icon, text and color to fit your brand.
caveats: Match the swatch label to the exact option value, or the badge won't bind to the variant.
Copy the styling pattern, not the competitor's trademark or content — avoid using their brand assets.
This copies a design element, not proven conversion results; test it on your own store.

cards.title: Make Global Theme Edits (Cart Icon and Notification Bubble)
cards.summary: Prompt Claude to change sitewide theme utilities like the cart icon style, add a selection of preset icons, and customize the cart count bubble.
cards.use_when: You want storewide cosmetic/UX changes (cart icon, cart count color, add-to-cart feedback) that aren't exposed as template-level settings.
steps: Prompt with a clear scope, e.g.: 'Change the shopping cart icon and let me pick from pre-selected icons like cart, bag, trolley. Add a small animation when something is added to cart, and let me change the color of the number notification on the cart.'
Wait for Claude to report where the new controls live (the example placed them under Header > Utilities).
In the theme editor, go to the reported location and select the new icon style and set the cart count background and number colors.
Test add-to-cart feedback on the storefront.
caveats: The presenter's bundle of instructions produced the icons and colors but failed to implement the requested add-to-cart animation — too many instructions at once is the suggested cause.
If a requested feature doesn't appear, break it into a single focused follow-up prompt rather than assuming it worked.

cards.title: Give Claude One Change at a Time, Not a Bundle
cards.summary: Split AI theme requests into single focused prompts, because bundling several changes risks partial or failed implementation.
cards.use_when: You are planning a series of theme or PDP edits and deciding how to sequence prompts.
steps: Decide the single change you want (e.g. change the cart icon only).
Write a prompt scoped to that one change.
Verify the result in the theme editor before moving on.
If a bundled prompt (like the cart icon + animation + count color request) partially fails, re-run the missing piece as its own prompt.
Track which changes succeeded so you can re-issue the failed ones.
caveats: This is the presenter's observed lesson from a request that partially failed, not a hard rule — a clearly related bundle can still work but is riskier.

cards.title: Manage Claude Usage Limits During Heavy Theme Coding
cards.summary: Plan for hitting Claude's usage limit and cooldown when running many theme edits.
cards.use_when: You are doing multi-hour AI theme work and want to avoid running out mid-task.
steps: Watch for the usage-limit warning (the example reported '90% of your limit used').
When you hit the limit, pause theme coding — the source states it resets in about an hour.
Use the cooldown to plan the next changes or review already-generated output.
Batch your most important edits earlier in a session before the limit approaches.
caveats: The reset window (about an hour) and limit percentage are the source's observation and may change with Claude's plans — verify current limits.

cards.title: Publish a Claude-Edited Theme and Maintain an Up-to-Date Working Copy
cards.summary: Publish your edited duplicate safely, then re-duplicate the live theme for the next round of edits.
cards.use_when: Your AI-edited theme or template is validated and you are ready to push it live.
steps: In Shopify, confirm the duplicate theme looks correct before publishing.
Click Publish on the edited theme; the previously live theme moves to unpublished.
Treat theme file edits as saved automatically in the theme files — only in-editor content/setting changes need saving.
For the next round of work, duplicate the now-live theme so your working copy is the most current, then edit and republish that.
caveats: Publishing is the riskiest step — the source calls it the scariest part of the process.
Skipping the re-duplicate step means you could edit a stale copy and overwrite newer live changes.

editorial_cleanup: Qualified sampled deployment, plugin-removal and point-in-time access instructions.
